\section{Prompt Templates}
\label{app:prompts}

We show representative prompt examples for each formulation. All examples use the same input instance for comparability.

\paragraph{CLS (per-test classification).}
\begin{verbatim}
System: You are a code verifier. Given a
code patch and a test name, predict whether
the test will pass or fail when run against
the patched code.

User:
## Patch (git diff)
<patch content>
[... truncated ...]

## Test
test_boundary_check

Will this test pass or fail?

Target: pass
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{CWM (execution simulation).}
\begin{verbatim}
System: You are a code execution simulator.
Given a code snippet and a test case,
predict the execution result.

User:
## Code
<code content>
[... truncated ...]

## Test
test_boundary_check

What is the execution result?

Target: PASS: test completed successfully
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{TRAJ (trajectory scoring).}
\begin{verbatim}
System: You are a code repair verifier.
Given the code patch and test summary,
predict whether all tests pass (resolved)
or any test fails (unresolved).

User:
[Code]
<patch content>
[... truncated ...]

[Test Summary]
<all test names and descriptions>

Target: resolved
\end{verbatim}

\cls{} and \cwm{} share the same input format (one code--test pair per instance); \cls{} produces a single token (\texttt{pass}/\texttt{fail}), while \cwm{} generates a variable-length execution trace. \traj{} receives all tests concatenated and produces a single token (\texttt{resolved}/\texttt{unresolved}).

1	\begin{abstract}
2	LLM-based program repair increasingly relies on generating multiple candidate patches and selecting the best via a verifier. Execution-based verification is reliable but expensive; three execution-free alternatives have emerged: per-test binary classification (\cls{}), execution output generation (\cwm{}), and trajectory-level patch scoring (\traj{}). No prior work compares these formulations under matched conditions.
3	
4	We present the first systematic comparison across two representative code LLM families (Qwen3, DeepSeek-Coder), two complexity levels, and multiple seeds under ${\leq}$8B LoRA fine-tuning. At function level, \cls{} and \cwm{} are statistically equivalent across both families (TOST, 5 seeds): classification is not inherently easier than generation when outputs are short. \traj{} parity is model-dependent. At repository level, a significant interaction ($z{=}-23.7$, DeepSeek-Coder) confirms this equivalence collapses: the \cls{}--\cwm{} gap widens to 18--26\pp{} across 3 seeds per model under our ${\leq}$8B LoRA protocol in variant-level evaluation, driven by format collapse in generation-based simulation. Gap magnitude depends on multiple confounds.
5	
6	Error complementarity and a failure mode taxonomy motivate complexity-aware formulation routing over uniform selection.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
\item \textbf{Formulation near-equivalence at low complexity.} At function level, \cls{} and \cwm{} achieve statistical equivalence across two representative code LLM families; \traj{} reaches parity on Qwen3 but exceeds the equivalence margin on DeepSeek-Coder. Per-test classification matches trajectory-level accuracy on Qwen3 (TRAJ parity is model-dependent) while providing per-test diagnostic signal (\S\ref{sec:func_results}, \S\ref{sec:equivalence}).

\item \textbf{Complexity-dependent divergence.} A significant interaction ($z{=}-23.7$, $n{=}56{,}480$, DeepSeek-Coder) confirms that formulations equivalent at function level (${\leq}$1.3\pp{}) diverge by 18--26\pp{} at repository level under ${\leq}$8B LoRA fine-tuning, driven by format collapse---four targeted interventions all fail to close the gap (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_analysis}(g)). Variant-level analysis reveals three failure modes consistent across model families, though gap magnitude depends on limited seed coverage and multiple confounds (\S\ref{sec:repo}, \S\ref{sec:threats}).

\item \textbf{Error complementarity.} \cls{} and \cwm{} exhibit partially complementary error patterns at function level (oracle: 90.63\%, 95\% CI [89.3\%, 91.9\%]; single-seed); at repo level, oracle routing reaches 95.83\% variant accuracy (+14.58\pp{}; single-seed), the strongest practical argument for exploring formulation-level tradeoffs (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
\end{itemize}
tool_args.new_string:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
\item \textbf{Complexity-governed formulation choice.} We establish a three-layer structure: (1)~fine-tuning is necessary (35--36\pp{} gains); (2)~at function level, formulations are near-equivalent---\cls{} and \cwm{} achieve statistical equivalence (TOST $p{=}0.007$, Holm-corrected) across both families, while \traj{} parity differs between families; (3)~at repository level under ${\leq}$8B LoRA, this equivalence collapses ($z{=}-23.7$, DeepSeek-Coder), with \cwm{} falling 18--26\pp{} below \cls{}, driven by format collapse---four interventions all fail to close the gap. The TOST framework demonstrates strict equivalence rather than mere non-significance (\S\ref{sec:equivalence}, \S\ref{sec:repo}).

\item \textbf{Error complementarity.} \cls{} and \cwm{} exhibit partially complementary error patterns at function level (oracle: 90.63\%, 95\% CI [89.3\%, 91.9\%]; single-seed); at repo level, oracle routing reaches 95.83\% variant accuracy (+14.58\pp{}; single-seed), the strongest practical argument for exploring formulation-level tradeoffs (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
\end{itemize}
